secondaryKeywords: is there anything new in seo
h1: Every 'Innovative' SEO Tactic We've Seen Was a Repackaged Basic
metaTitle: The Most Innovative SEO Tactics Are Usually Old
metaDescription: Most innovative SEO tactics are old ideas in new packaging. Here are the two things that are genuinely new since 2023, and eight that only sound new.
answer: Almost none of them are new. Eight tactics currently sold as innovative SEO are renamed basics — topic clusters, pruning, refreshing, PR, reading the SERP. Two things are genuinely new since 2023: consolidating your entity so AI systems describe you consistently, and covering the sub-queries an AI fans a question out into.
takeaways: Eight of the tactics on every 2026 conference slide have older names. Pricing them as new work is the industry's most reliable margin.
Novelty sells because it justifies a call, a rate rise and a slide. Compounding doesn't, because the credit is diffuse and the payoff is late.
**Entity consolidation** is genuinely new in kind: you're aligning claims on properties you don't own, for a reader that is a model rather than a person.
**Query fan-out** breaks the feedback loop. One question becomes several machine queries, and you can't see them in Search Console. Anyone who says they can measure it precisely is guessing.

sections.h2: Eight tactics that are old work in a new jacket
body: We've been pitched, sold and occasionally seduced by every one of these. Each is real work worth doing. None of them is new, and the renaming is doing a lot of commercial labour that the underlying idea never asked for.
The test is simple: if you can describe a tactic to a marketer from 2015 and they nod rather than blink, it isn't new.

callout.title: Old doesn't mean wrong
callout.body: Every row above is work we do and bill for. The objection isn't to the practice, it's to the pricing of a rename as an innovation — and to the founder who ends up paying twice because nobody told them their last agency already did this under a different heading.

body: It isn't a conspiracy. It's an incentive structure, and once you can see it you can price around it.

A named new tactic is a reason to send an email, book a call, justify a rate rise, and fill a conference slot. 'We're going to keep doing the same competent work for another eleven months' is a true sentence that has never once won a pitch. Nobody has ever been given a stage for the eighteenth consecutive month of a publishing cadence, which is a shame, because that's where the compounding lives.
bullets: **Agencies with churn need novelty.** If clients leave at month nine, you need something that makes month nine feel like month one. A new tactic is the cheapest way to manufacture that feeling.

**Tool vendors need categories.** Naming a practice creates a product line, a comparison page and a search term nobody else owns yet. That's a rational business decision and it's why half the vocabulary exists.
**Conferences need programming.** Forty slots a year, and 'the basics, again, correctly' fills none of them.
**Founders want it to be true.** A new tactic implies your flat quarter wasn't your fault — the rules changed. That's a far more comfortable story than 'we published four thin pages and stopped'.
**And yes, we're implicated.** We're a marketing agency writing marketing content. The temptation to name something and claim it is constant. This article is us resisting it on a good day.

sections.h2: The first genuinely new thing: entity consolidation
body: Here's what changed, and why it's different in kind rather than degree.

Classic SEO optimised a URL against a query. Everything you touched, you owned. AI assistants and AI Overviews don't work that way — they assemble a description of your company from everything written about it anywhere, then answer from that composite. The unit of work moves from the page to the entity, and most of the entity lives on properties you don't control.

The honest ancestor here is local SEO's obsession with consistent name, address and phone across directories. We're not going to pretend that's unrelated — it's the same instinct. What's different is the scope and the reader. It now applies to every factual claim about you: what you sell, what you charge, who you serve, which cities you operate in, who runs the company. And the reader is a language model, which doesn't shrug at contradictory sources. It picks one, states it confidently, and repeats it to your prospect.

subs.h3: What the work actually looks like
bullets: Decide your canonical facts and write them in plain declarative sentences. Not brand copy — sentences a machine can lift without interpreting. 'SEO starts at ₹75,000 per month' beats 'flexible pricing tailored to your needs', which parses to nothing.
State them explicitly on crawlable pages: an about page with real names, a pricing page with real numbers, a services page that names the deliverables.
Then fix the third parties. Stale directory entries, an old press release with a superseded price, a LinkedIn description written by a founder in 2021, a review site listing a service you dropped.
Add `Organization` schema and keep its values identical to the prose. Contradicting yourself in your own markup is a strangely common own goal.
Keep the phrasing consistent across all of it. Retrieval systems reconcile conflicting sources badly, so give them nothing to reconcile.

subs.h3: How to test it in ten minutes
body: Ask three different assistants to describe your company and what it charges. Write down every wrong statement, then trace each one to its source — it's almost always a stale listing, an old article, or a page on your own site that hedges instead of stating.

If you're vague about pricing on your own site, a model will fill the gap with a guess, and the guess will be wrong and confident. That's the strongest practical argument for publishing your prices that we've encountered, and it's why ours are on the site rather than behind a form.

callout.title: The failure mode nobody warns you about
callout.body: You can be described inaccurately by a system that never crawled your site. A prospect asks an assistant about you, gets a two-year-old price and a service you no longer offer, and decides against a call. There's no impression, no click and no line in any report. You simply never hear from them.

sections.h2: The second: query fan-out, and what it does to coverage
body: Google has described its AI Mode as using a query fan-out technique — taking one question, issuing several related searches across subtopics and sources, then synthesising an answer from the results. Assistants do their own version of the same thing.

That changes what 'ranking for a query' means. A single user question becomes several machine queries you never see. Your page can be the best answer to the question as asked and still be absent from the response, because the citation went to whoever answered sub-question three about pricing, or the exception, or the comparison against the obvious alternative.

So coverage stops meaning keyword variants and starts meaning decomposition. Take the question your page targets, break it into the six or eight things a careful person would want to know underneath it — how much, how long, what breaks, compared to what, what if I'm in this specific situation — and answer each one, in its own section, self-containedly. Passages start to matter more than pages, because a passage is what gets retrieved.

The uncomfortable consequence is measurement. You cannot see the fan-out queries in Search Console. You often can't see the original question either. The clean feedback loop that made SEO the most accountable channel in marketing is partially broken for this surface, nobody has a good substitute yet, and anybody selling you precise attribution for AI citations is selling you a modelled number with a confident face on it. We'd rather say that than invoice for it — the broader argument is in [is generative engine optimization real](/journal/is-generative-engine-optimization-real).

sections.h2: The things we're not doing yet, and why
body: Restraint is a tactic too, and it's the only one that gets cheaper the longer you hold it.
bullets: **[llms.txt](/glossary/llms-txt)** — a proposed convention for telling AI systems what's on your site. We've seen no confirmation that the major assistants actually consume it. It takes about an hour to add, so add it if the hour is free. Don't build a plan around it and don't pay anyone a retainer line for it.

**Publishing at volume to win citations.** Volume without differentiation is exactly the pattern Google names as scaled content abuse, and the penalty lands on the whole domain rather than the thin pages. We drew the line in [programmatic SEO and the scaled content line](/journal/programmatic-seo-and-the-scaled-content-line).
**Schema on everything.** Structured data helps machines parse what's already there. It does not manufacture authority, and no amount of markup makes a weak page a strong one.

**A separate 'AI visibility' retainer.** Ask what's in it. If the answer is clear factual pages, consistent entity data, structured answers and earned mentions, you're being quoted twice for work that was already in the SEO scope.
**Chasing every core update with a rewrite.** Rankings wobble for a fortnight after an update while the index settles. Rewriting in week one means rewriting against noise.

sections.h2: How to test a new tactic without risking the site
body: When something genuinely new does turn up — and twice in three years, something has — you want to try it without betting the domain on a stranger's blog post. Six rules, and we hold to them on our own site first.
numbered: **Ring-fence it.** One directory, or 5–10% of URLs. Never your top twenty pages by revenue, never the templates those pages share. If the tactic is site-wide by nature, that's a reason for more caution, not less.
**One variable, one window.** Change the template and the publishing cadence in the same month and you've learned precisely nothing at the end of it.
**Write the kill criteria before you start.** Metric, threshold, date. 'Let's see how it goes' is how a test quietly becomes a permanent feature nobody can justify.
**Keep the rollback.** Version the old template, keep the old copy, and use `noindex` before you delete so a reversal doesn't cost you the URL and its history.
**Measure against a control.** Comparable untouched pages in the same section. Site-wide traffic in a month that contained a core update tells you about the update, not about your test.
**Cap it in time.** Ninety days, then a decision: keep, kill, or extend once with a stated reason. Tests that run indefinitely aren't tests, they're habits.

callout.title: Our own hit rate
callout.body: Of the tactics we've tested this way, most produce nothing distinguishable from noise, a few produce a small durable gain, and roughly one in ten is worth building into the standard process. We give this as a shape rather than a percentage because we run tests to make decisions, not to generate statistics for a blog post.

sections.h2: Three questions we ask before billing anyone for something new
body: Cheap filters, applied in about ninety seconds, on a call.
numbered: **What's the old name for this?** If there is one, price it as the old thing and check whether your previous agency already did it. If there genuinely isn't one, keep listening — that's rare and interesting.

**What breaks if it's wrong?** Reversible on twenty pages is a test. Irreversible across the site — a URL restructure, a mass deletion, a migration — is a bet, and bets get made with evidence rather than enthusiasm.

**Who profits from me believing this?** A tool vendor defining a category, an agency with a churn problem, a conference with slots to fill. None of those make the claim false. They do tell you how much scepticism to bring.

sections.h2: What we'd spend the hour on instead
body: If you have one hour and a choice between reading about a tactic named this quarter and doing something dull, do the dull thing. In order of what usually pays fastest:

Pull your striking-distance list out of Search Console and fix the top five pages. Add internal links from your strongest pages to the ones you actually want ranked. Delete or merge everything that hasn't earned a visit in a year. Test your site on a mid-range Android phone on a 4G connection, because that is what most of India is browsing on, and fix whatever takes more than three seconds. Ring one customer, record the call with permission, and use their actual words instead of the ones in your brief.

None of that will get you invited to speak anywhere. All of it compounds, and the compounding is the part competitors can't copy by reading a slide. Whether covering a subject properly is even a real ranking property is worth arguing about too — we did, in [does topical authority actually exist](/journal/does-topical-authority-actually-exist).

We take three clients a month and we guarantee movement against your own frozen trailing-90-day organic lead baseline, not a position on a page. That constraint is why we're allergic to novelty: an unproven tactic costs us free months, not you. It turns out the fastest way to make an agency conservative about tactics is to make it liable for the results.

faqs.q: Is there anything genuinely new in SEO?
faqs.a: Two things since 2023, by our count. Entity consolidation — making the facts about your company consistent everywhere, because AI systems describe you from sources you don't own. And query fan-out coverage — answering the sub-questions a machine breaks your topic into. Everything else on the 2026 slides has an older name.

faqs.q: What are the most advanced SEO techniques that actually work?
faqs.a: The ones that are boring and specific: rescuing pages already ranking 8–20, merging pages that compete with each other, internal links with descriptive anchors, and earning coverage from publications that would have covered you anyway. Advanced usually means executed properly, not exotic.

faqs.q: Should I add llms.txt to my site?
faqs.a: If you have a spare hour, sure. We've seen no confirmation that major assistants consume it, so treat it as a cheap option rather than a plan. If an agency has it as a priced line item on a retainer, ask what else on that invoice is priced the same way.

faqs.q: How do I test a new SEO tactic safely?
faqs.a: Ring-fence it to 5–10% of URLs and never your top revenue pages. Change one variable. Write down the metric, threshold and review date before you start. Keep a rollback, use noindex before deleting, measure against untouched control pages, and cap the test at 90 days.

faqs.q: Why does the SEO industry keep renaming old tactics?
faqs.a: Because novelty is sellable and compounding isn't. A named tactic justifies an email, a rate rise and a conference slot. 'Keep doing the same competent work for another eleven months' is true, correct, and has never won a pitch in the history of the industry.

faqs.q: Do creative or unusual SEO ideas ever beat the basics?
faqs.a: Occasionally, and usually because they're a genuinely good piece of PR rather than a search tactic. A data study nobody else could produce earns links the basics can't. But it works as an addition to competent fundamentals, never as a replacement for them.
